headline: Reviewed FY27 property tax information, including the tax shift, exemptions, and a $1 million Targeted Tax Relief Program; no vote taken.
summary: The committee reviewed property assessments, tax classifications, exemptions, and the Targeted Tax Relief Program, which received $1 million in initial funding. No vote or formal recommendation was recorded.

5:00 PM Meeting called to order on October 20, 2026, in Hybrid Room 200, 36 Court Street, 
Springfield, MA 01103. 
 
Public Portion 
 1. Discussion of FY27 Preliminary Tax Rate Information 
On October 20, 2026, the Finance Committee and Tax Rate Committee, chaired by Councilor 
Zaida Govan, met to review the FY2027 property tax classification process. Jessica Guerra, 
Chair of the Board of Assessors, presented an overview of property assessments, Proposition 2½, 
tax levy limits, new growth, and the responsibilities of the Board of Assessors, Department of 
Revenue, and City Council. Springfield has approximately 46,000 taxable parcels and personal 
property accounts. FY2026 assessed values increased 7.81%, with an average single-family 
assessment of $275,000, an average tax bill of $4,255, and a residential tax rate of $15.46 per 
$1,000. The maximum tax shift factor of 1.75 resulted in residential properties paying 61% of the 
levy and commercial, industrial, and personal property paying 39%. The shift redistributes the 
tax burden without increasing the total levy. Final FY2027 assessments and new growth figures 
remain pending Department of Revenue approval. 
 
The committee reviewed available property tax exemptions for qualifying seniors, veterans, 
surviving spouses, and residents with disabilities, along with the state Circuit Breaker Tax 
Credit. The newly established Targeted Tax Relief Program received $1 million in initial funding 
to assist eligible low-income elderly or disabled homeowners. Applications opened October 13 
and close November 13, 2026, with individual applications scheduled for review beginning 
November 20. Discussion addressed increasing public awareness through neighborhood 
councils, libraries, and community outreach.
Additional discussion focused on property affordability, the impact of tax classifications on 
homeowners and businesses, redevelopment of vacant properties, small business assistance, and 
opportunities to increase state and federal funding. Members requested examples illustrating how 
different tax factors would affect residential and commercial tax bills. City officials reported an 
estimated 96% to 97% property tax collection rate and confirmed that FY2027 property tax 
revenues remain on track with budget projections. Additional new growth revenue may be 
directed toward the overlay account for abatements. The committee also reviewed financial 
reserves and anticipated expenses associated with the recent microburst, with a funding request 
expected following free cash certification. 
 
The next Tax Rate Committee meeting is scheduled for November 12, 2026, when updated 
assessments and tax factor options are expected to be presented. The City Council Tax 
Classification Public Hearing is scheduled for November 24, 2026. No formal recommendation 
or vote was recorded. The meeting adjourned at 5:55 p.m.
